en: He introduces the characteristics of women belonging to the *lāmā* class, beginning with the words "Now," and so forth. *Padmanarteśvara* is Amitābha. *Chāgala* means simply a goat (*chagala*). *Ḍākinī* refers to a *ḍākinī*. *Tathāgata* is Vairocana. *Lomaśā* means one whose body is covered with hair. *Śakula* is a *śaṣkulī*; it is a line having that shape. *Vināyaka* is Śrī Saṃvara. She is endowed with the extreme steadfastness of Akṣobhya.
Having joined the two hands in the hollowed gesture (*saṃpuṭa*), slightly bending the two thumbs and bringing the tips of the other fingers together so they touch, this is the *padma-mudrā*.

The *kūrma-mudrā* is formed by extending one hand and placing the other hand above it, with the fingers contracted like a tortoise (*kūrma*). These two mudrās constitute the *jina-mudrā*, performed by the practitioner in the gesture of holding the hem of the garment with the left arm drawn back while the garment hangs from the left shoulder. Alternatively, according to the reading "one should worship" (*arcayet*), the *jina-mudrā* is so called because he who is worshipped is the Jina himself; this is expressed through a figurative turn of phrase. These two mudrās should be given as their corresponding counter-mudrās (*pratimudrā*) to the Yoginī.

Regarding "the *śūla* mudrā": by pressing the little finger with the thumb and extending the other fingers upward; while dancing in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) with the left foot drawn up, turning with the left [hand] is the counter-mudrā (*pratimudrā*) of the Yoginī. "Worship" (*pūjā*) refers to the time of worship. "Of the Lokeśvarīs" means of those belonging to the family of Amitābha. "Bound with a ribbon" (*paṭṭabaddha*) means a single line like a ribbon tied on the forehead.
By pressing all the fingers with the thumb and extending the index finger upward, one forms the *śakti* mudrā.
The *ghaṇṭā* mudrā is formed by the gesture of ringing a bell.
"Second" means the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*). Having performed that, one turns around; the same applies to the subsequent [seals].

Having formed the *vajrāñjali*, one raises the two middle fingers, encircles the two ring fingers with the two index fingers, straightens the two thumbs, and holds them near the face—this is the *vaktramudrā* (face seal).

Having crossed the ring fingers and placed the thumbs between them in the shape of a ring, with the little and middle fingers joined like needles and the middle fingers [joined] at their sides, one should bend the index fingers and place them on the third joint; this is called the *vaktramudrā* (face-mudrā) in the *Trisamayarājatantre*. [Note:

In some versions, the reading is *cakramudrām* (wheel-mudrā). In that case, with the hands turned upward, one should place the thumbs upon the nails of the middle and ring fingers; this is the *cakramudrā*.]

Regarding the *śaṅkhamudrā*: having contracted the middle, ring, and little fingers, one forms the gesture of a conch by extending the thumb and forefinger. "In the same way" means with the left hand; thus it is called the *pratimudrā*, as previously described. Regarding "on the festival day" (*parvaṇi*), this refers to a time of meritorious celebration. "Terrible" (*karālā*) means jagged. Having raised the left hand and placed the right elbow upon it, one should hold the right hand with the thumb and forefinger extended and the other three fingers contracted; this is the *nāgamudrā*. "As before" means that the left hand serves as the *pratimudrā*.

Generally, these characteristics have been described for those of the *lāmā* class; however, it is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) that these should also be understood to apply to the thirty-seven yoginīs.
The fifteenth Mañjarī in the Āmnāyamañjarī, the commentary on the Śrīsampuṭa.
